paragraphs: I [[abandoned|abandon]] my job at a [[publishing]] house in June, after eight years of reading other people's [[prose]]. My [[salary]] was good, the [[economy]] was uncertain, and everyone said it was a [[mad]] decision. I had spent years correcting a [[phrase]] on every [[page]], and my [[background]] was in books, not in flour. My last [[editorial]] meeting ended with a shrug and a [[joke]] about people who open bakeries. So I took the train [[back]] to the town where I grew up.

My grandmother's shop stood on the [[square]], and she had run it [[daily]] for forty years. Her [[cake]] and [[pudding]] were famous, and her [[plum]] tart sold out before noon. She counted [[calorie]]s for nobody and [[quality]] for everything. I wanted to [[earn]] my living there, though the [[habit]] of office life was hard to break.

The [[rear]] room was [[damp]], and the [[narrow]] stairs creaked under every tray. We cleared years of dust with a [[vacuum]] and found an old [[store]] of tins behind the [[wall]]. A [[kit]] of pastry tools hung by the window, most of them older than I was. The [[streetlight]] outside made the whole window glow after closing time, though the damp had done [[damage]] to the frame. A [[gate]] at the side let in the morning light, and we kept it open.

Behind the shop was a [[horticultural]] tangle of herbs, and mint and thyme [[abound]] there. My grandmother [[gathered|gather]] mint every morning, and I learned to [[observe]] which beds stayed wet. The [[earth]] there was dark, and in [[damp]] weather the roses [[faded|fade]] early. A [[rabbit]] came at dusk to eat the lettuce, and a late frost could [[kill]] the herbs. We mowed the small lawn together, and she never let me use the noisy machine.

My first [[co-worker]] was a [[budding]] baker named Lili, [[recruited|recruit]] from the technical school. She had real [[talent]] and was never [[jealous]] of anyone's recipes. Her [[kin]] ran a [[lamb]] farm outside town, and her uncle delivered meat twice a week. A [[lone]] customer who came every day for a [[packet]] of biscuits became our most loyal [[supporter]].

On Saturdays we cleared the tables for a reading club, and I read stories about a [[safari]] and a [[knight]]. The children preferred the one about a [[king]] who [[buried|bury]] his [[relic]] under a [[volcano]], and a story about a [[heaven]] made of bread. We acted out a [[raft]] trip and a [[camp]] on the moon, and nobody minded the plot. For an hour the shop became a place where a [[saint]] could sit beside a [[rabbit]].

In July a [[landowner]] announced a [[skyscraper]] on the [[square]], and the town [[declared|declare]] itself open for business. The [[major]] [[stakeholder]] was a company nobody in the street had heard of. A [[liberal]] councillor said the plan needed a public [[petition]], not a private [[warrant]]. We gathered signatures and stood at the [[gate]] every morning.

Then a [[clue]] appeared: an [[unnamed]] letter said the company had bought land under a false name. The [[conspiracy]] was [[dense]] with detail, and the [[wrongdoing]] went back years. Someone [[sneaked|sneak]] into our yard one night and left a box of papers as [[bait]]. The tower would [[impinge]] on the light that reached the square, and the company's interests were never [[aligned]] with ours. I began to [[name]] the people behind it, though that was dangerous.

Our lawyer obtained a [[warrant]] to see the accounts, and the figures [[worsened|worsen]] the company's position. A [[clawback]] clause in the contract was the [[trigger]] for the whole dispute. It was [[unacceptable]] that a [[danger]] of this size sat on the [[edge]] of the square, and the accounts had a [[gaping]] hole. Without public support the deal would [[disintegrate]], and the [[proportion]] of local shops would fall. The two issues were [[tied|tie]] together, and no one could separate them.

On the first Sunday in August I ran a [[race]] through the town, my first as a [[runner]] in twenty years. I kept a slow [[pace]], passed the [[half]] mark, and at three [[quarters|quarter]] of the way wanted to stop. A [[hale]] old man in a [[uniform]] ran beside me and invited me to a [[joint]] class in [[self-defence]]. I did not [[believe]] I could finish, but the [[prospect]] of the shop's door kept me moving.

The shop's [[sale]]s rose in August, and our [[proficiency]] with the old oven finally showed. Lili had the [[ability]] to [[create]] a new cake from whatever was left in the [[store]], and to [[pack]] the bread before I finished counting. We [[exchanged|exchange]] recipes with a café across the street, a [[mutual]] arrangement that helped both of us. I began to [[believe]] we could [[achieve]] something real, though a [[fad]] for sourdough helped more than skill. Most new cafés are a [[fad]], a friend said; ours had a [[theory]] behind it. It was hard to [[balance]] the books and the ovens, but we managed.

In September my grandmother fell [[ill]], and her [[thinness]] frightened me. She sat by the window with her [[hair]] uncombed, and I gave her a [[haircut]] on the back step. Her [[jaw]] was set and her [[face]] calm, and she refused to let me [[wake]] the doctor. I felt the floor [[quake]] under me the day she could not get up. She told me to stay [[calm]] and to keep the shop open.

At the town meeting the [[rage]] was [[viscerally]] real, and two neighbours had a [[nasty]] [[quarrel]]. It is easy to [[oversimplify]] such a fight, but the [[methodology]] of the developer's survey was [[wholly]] dishonest. An [[introductory]] speech by the mayor was [[goal-focused]] and said nothing at all, which I would [[call]] a waste of ten minutes. I heard [[prejudice]] in my own voice too, and that was the worst part.

In October a food [[magazine]] sent a writer to [[name]] us one of the best bakeries in the [[nation]]. The article called us [[rising]] stars, and the [[label]] on our window suddenly mattered. A [[screener]] from the magazine asked to [[retake]] the photographs because the light was wrong. We built a three-[[tier]] cake for the photograph, and it collapsed on the way out. The [[key]] to the article was a single line, printed in [[ink]]: the shop was not [[unrealistically]] perfect.

That same week someone broke in and [[took|take]] the cash box from the [[safe]]. We found a [[back-up]] of the accounts on an old drive, which was a small [[gain]]. The police said the [[lack]] of a camera made the case hard. The bank had also begun to [[backload]] its fees onto small shops like ours. I learned to [[label]] every box and to count the till twice.

The Saturday market was a [[game]] of patience, and it was not [[easy]] to sell bread beside cheap cakes. A [[war]] of signs had started on the street, and the [[welfare]] of the older shopkeepers depended on the outcome. My grandmother had spent a month in the [[ward]] after a bad winter, and she never forgot the nurses. She said a town that protects its weakest is worth more than one with a tall tower. The [[damn]] thing about small towns, she added, is that everyone knows your name.

The children [[continued|continue]] the reading club through the winter, and their [[zeal]] gave me [[zest]] for the work. Their [[idea]] of a party included a [[dance]] and a [[bizarre]] game they [[dubbed|dub]] the key dance. A [[fact]] we had not expected was that the [[quantity]] of bread they ate doubled. The [[labor]] of kneading had doubled too, and the [[factor]] behind it was simple: hungry children learn better. [[Above]] the shop, my grandmother kept a [[wardrobe]] of old clothes and a pair of [[jeans]] that no longer fit. A [[tailor]] had made them, she said, and clothes, like towns, could be adjusted.

In December I began to see a [[pattern]] in our days, and the [[prospect]] of spring did not [[obscure]] the hard parts. A good baker needs [[tact]] as much as flour, she said, and I was [[unable]] to argue. The town had [[joined|join]] the petition, the tower was never built, and the road to the station still ran [[downhill]] past our door. I still [[labour]] over the oven at six, and I have never missed the office. The shop was not [[naked]] ambition; it was simply work, done well, and she spoke of its [[transcendence]] without ever using the word. [[About]] half my old colleagues thought I was mad, and the other half asked for a job.
